description: Team Polaris Path builds Eternal Dawn, a lunar landing-site navigator for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. Using real NASA JPL DE421 data, it shows Sun and Earth visibility at any Moon site, compares landing sites, and includes PP-1, a concept rover, plus a playable stone-collection game. Skills: architecture, computational design, 3D modelling, web development.
summary:
Eternal Dawn is an interactive, browser-based tool that helps mission planners and students choose safe Moon landing sites in seconds. For any site and landing date, it shows where the Sun and Earth sit in the local sky, hour by hour, using real NASA JPL DE421 ephemeris data for 2027–2028. This answers the two questions that decide a lunar surface mission: will the lander get sunlight for power, and will it see Earth for direct radio contact?

Users can compare 16 landing sites side by side, explore a 3D Moon with the live Earth–Moon distance, and browse an atlas of 11 real rovers with the distances they drove. We also designed PP-1 Polaris Prospector, a concept sample-collection rover, and built Lunar Stone Run, a playable game where users drive PP-1, collect and measure Moon stones, and contribute to a fleet goal.

This matters for Artemis and other south-pole missions, where low Sun angles, long shadows and limited Earth visibility make landing-site choice critical. Eternal Dawn turns complex orbital data into clear visuals anyone can use, with no installation or login.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Eternal Dawn is a browser-based lunar landing-site navigator. For any site and landing date, it computes where the Sun and Earth sit in the local sky, hour by hour, and turns this into clear mission numbers: percentage of time in sunlight (solar power), percentage of time with Earth in view (direct radio contact), longest night and longest communications blackout. A Best Landing Window strip scores every landing day in the next 60 days, and a Compare tool ranks all 16 sites side by side, from Artemis south-pole ridges to Apollo, Chandrayaan-3, Chang'e and CLPS landing sites.

HOW IT WORKS

We processed NASA JPL DE421 ephemeris with the jplephem library to get Sun and Earth vectors every 2 hours for 2027–2028 in the Moon's principal-axis frame, including physical librations. The data is embedded in a single self-contained HTML file, and all sky geometry is computed live in the browser. A Data Check panel runs five physics tests on the data (Earth–Moon distance range, maximum Sun elevation at the south pole, far-side Earth visibility, 29.53-day synodic period, libration), and all five pass.

CREATIVITY

To make the data engaging, we designed PP-1 Polaris Prospector, a concept south-pole rover with a 6-wheel rocker-bogie, superelastic and metal-tile wheels, a microspine gripper, a front stone cage and a rear core drill, all original 3D models. In Lunar Stone Run, a playable game for desktop and mobile, users drive PP-1 for two minutes, collect at least five stones, and see each stone measured (mass, sphericity, Corey shape factor). A rover atlas shows 11 real lunar rovers and the distances they drove.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Landing-site choice decides whether a lander has power and can talk to Earth. Eternal Dawn lets mission teams, CLPS companies, students and the public shortlist sites in seconds with no installation or login, and turns NASA orbital data into visuals anyone can understand.

TOOLS

JavaScript, HTML/CSS, three.js (3D), Python with jplephem and NumPy (data processing), Playwright (testing and video capture), Blender (banner render). AI-assisted with Claude.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy of real NASA data versus clearly labelled approximations (horizon masks are generic, game terrain is simulated, PP-1 figures are estimates); low-angle south-pole lighting; far-side sites with no Earth view; mobile access; and an offline single-file app. Next step: add NASA LRO LOLA terrain for true horizons, slope and permanently-shadowed-region hazard scoring.
